messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 48

# The Flood

Marcus sits in the armchair across from me, his weathered hands folded in his lap. At seventy-four, he carries himself with the careful precision of someone accustomed to control—a tutor's habit, perhaps, of arranging thoughts in orderly sequence. But there is a brittleness to him now, a tension in his shoulders that suggests the order has fractured.

Three years ago, Marcus lived in a cottage in the valley with his partner of twenty-two years, David. The cottage was modest but beloved, filled with books and photographs spanning decades. Marcus had spent forty-five years tutoring mathematics to high school students, finding deep satisfaction in the moment when a struggling teenager suddenly grasped a concept. He had built a quiet, meaningful life.

Then came the storm. Three days of relentless rain in July transformed the creek that ran behind the cottage into a torrent. Marcus and David woke at two in the morning to water already seeping under the doors. The evacuation order came minutes later. In the chaos of gathering essentials, Marcus made a choice he replays constantly: he grabbed his laptop and a few photo albums but left behind decades of student notes, letters, the physical record of his professional identity. They escaped to higher ground with minutes to spare. The cottage was destroyed—swept downstream in the floodwaters along with everything else they couldn't carry.

Since then, Marcus exists in a state of hypervigilance disguised as normalcy. He checks weather forecasts obsessively, sometimes five or six times a day, his eyes scanning for storm warnings with the intensity he once reserved for parsing mathematical proofs. When clouds darken, his chest tightens. He has moved with David to a house on a hill, far from any waterway, but the geography offers no real comfort.

The intrusive memories arrive without warning. He'll be preparing a lesson plan for one of his three current tutoring students—he returned to work after a year, unable to bear the inactivity—and suddenly he's back in the cottage, water rising around his ankles, David's voice calling from another room. The memory is vivid and involuntary, pulling him away from the present moment. Sometimes it takes him several minutes to orient himself again to the dry room, the desk, the mathematics textbook open before him.

His sleep is fragmented. He lies awake listening to rain on the roof, cataloging each sound, assessing threat. When he does sleep, he dreams of water—always rising, always inevitable. He wakes gasping, sometimes waking David, who has learned to simply hold his hand in the darkness without speaking.

David has been patient, but Marcus senses the strain. He has withdrawn from the social life they once enjoyed. Dinner invitations are declined. The hiking group he belonged to no longer sees him. There seems little point in planning future trips or discussing retirement renovations. He cannot imagine a future with any certainty, cannot shake the bone-deep knowledge that everything can be taken in hours.

What troubles Marcus most is the erosion of something less tangible than the cottage. He has always been a man who solved problems, who helped others understand complexity. Now he finds himself unable to organize his own thoughts coherently. The confidence that defined his professional identity—the quiet certainty with which he once approached a difficult student or an elegant proof—has been replaced by a persistent doubt in his own capacity to understand anything at all.

He shows up to his tutoring sessions because commitment matters to him. But he moves through them now like someone reading from a script, present in body but fractured in mind, waiting always for the next storm.
